Russia-Ukraine War Romania Says It Shot Down 3rd Russian Drone in as Many Days As a result, Bucharest has expelled Russia’s ambassador to Romania, who called the protest over the drones a ‘propaganda stunt.’ Save Mark Us Preferred on Google Print Romanian President Nicusor Dan (L) and Moldovan President Maia Sandu (R) attend the Coalition of the Willing summit on security guarantees for Ukraine, at the Hotel des Invalides in Paris, France, on July 13, 2026. Teresa Suares/Pool Photo via AP Victoria Friedman 7/27/2026 | Updated: 7/27/2026 0:00 X 1 Romanian officials said one of their air force F-16s shot down a Russian UAV after it breached NATO airspace, the third such incident in three days. The Romanian Ministry of National Defense said in a July 26 statement that the drone was safely shot down some 7 miles northeast of Sulina, within Romania’s territorial waters. The ministry had confirmed that drones had also been shot down on Saturday and Friday . Romania, a NATO member, shares a 400-mile land border with Ukraine, and Russian UAVs have repeatedly violated its airspace during the more than four-year Ukraine war. In one incident in May, a Russian drone hit an apartment building, injuring two people. Russia is now stepping up attacks on Ukrainian ports ​across the Danube River. Related Stories Zelenskyy Says Russia Shared Satellite Imagery of US Bases With Iran Trump Says Russia and China Have Agreed Not to Sell Weapons to Iran Russia Blamed Romanian President Nicusor Dan said in an X post on July 26 that the UAV shot down on Friday was a Shahed drone, used by Russia in its attacks on Ukraine. He said that investigations into the origin of the drones shot down on Saturday and Sunday were ongoing. “Romania’s diplomatic protest against the Russian Federation will be based on these investigations,” Dan said. “It is inadmissible and intolerable for the Russian Federation to continue violating Romania’s airspace, which is, at the same time, NATO airspace and European Union airspace. Such actions are unacceptable, and we treat them with the utmost seriousness, alongside our allies.” NATO said ​additional details of Sunday’s incident were under investigation. “The shootdowns come as NATO, Romania, and other nations ​actively acquire ground-based interceptors to enhance allied and national air defense capabilities,” said U.S. Army Col. Martin O'Donnell, spokesman for ‌NATO’s ⁠military headquarters. Romania Dismisses Russian Ambassador The Romanian Ministry of Foreign Affairs said in a July 27 statement that it had summoned the Russian ambassador to Bucharest, Vladimir Lipaev, to discuss the incidents. The ministry said the call came “as a firm reaction to the repeated violations of Romania’s airspace” between July 24 and 26, during which the Romanian military “shot down three drones that had entered the national territory without authorization.” Lipaev was shown pieces of the UAV destroyed over Romanian territory, which initial investigations conducted by the Prosecutor’s Office confirmed were of Russian origin, the statement said. “It was emphasized that it is absolutely inadmissible and intolerable for the Russian Federation to continue violating Romanian airspace, which is equally NATO and European Union airspace,” the ministry said. “The Romanian side highlighted that the Russian Federation bears sole responsibility for all these serious incidents and for the deterioration of the regional security environment.” The Ministry of Foreign Affairs said it had dismissed the Russian ambassador and gave Lipaev five days to leave Romania. ‘Propaganda Stunt’ Lipaev protested the alleged Russian violations of Romanian airspace. “It’s clear that this is a propaganda stunt, the purpose of which is to prevent further attacks by Russian armed forces on Ukrainian port infrastructure on the Danube and the Black Sea, which is actively used by NATO to supply weapons and equipment to the Ukrainian Armed Forces through Romanian territory,” the ambassador told Russian state-run news agency TASS on July 27. Lipaev said Bucharest had leveled “unfounded, unsubstantiated accusations against Russia,” had not disclosed technical details of the drones that would allow them to be identified, and had not provided evidence of their origin. “The unjustified expulsion of an embassy employee will not go unanswered by Russia,” Lipaev said. Reuters contributed to this report. https://www.jpost.com/travel/article-905.text: Sunday, August 16, is 3 Elul. It is not only the yahrzeit of Rabbi Abraham Isaac HaCohen Kook, the first chief rabbi of Israel and the greatest spiritual architect of religious Zionism. It is also an invitation to travel. Not merely through his books, but through landscapes.The winding country roads of Latvia and Lithuania, lined with silver birch forests and bordered by quiet rivers, still seem to whisper his story. The scent of wet earth after a summer shower, the rustling of flax fields in the wind, the silence of forgotten Jewish cemeteries, all preserve echoes of a man who believed that holiness was not hidden from the changing world but revealed through it.To understand Rabbi Kook, opening his books Orot or Igrot HaRe'iyah is not enough. We must walk where he walked, breathe the same northern air, and stand before the remnants of the communities that shaped his soul. Several Israeli religious tour operators organize heritage journeys following Rabbi Kook's footsteps. Their tours continue to attract Jewish travelers eager to discover not only the biography of a towering rabbinic figure but also the landscapes from which his revolutionary ideas emerged.GrivaNearly 160 years ago, a baby was born in the small town of Griva, today a neighborhood of Daugavpils in southeastern Latvia. His parents named him Abraham Isaac, but affectionately called him “Yatzki.”When little Yatzki was only three, he attended the local cheder. There he invented a game: He lined up the children with their small satchels across their shoulders, as though preparing for a long expedition. Then he asked them to call out: “Where are we going?” And he would shout back: “To Eretz Israel!”It was a child's game, yet in hindsight it seems almost prophetic.That game took place in the courtyard of the Kaddish Synagogue, which still stands today after careful restoration. Here, his parents used to pray, and the young prodigy astonished the community. At nine, he was already delivering sermons from its pulpit, and by 11 he had begun writing a commentary on the Song of Songs.Visitors to the synagogue at Cietokšna 38 today will find commemorative plaques honoring Rabbi Kook on the synagogue's exterior. Joining the Mincha prayer service inside these ancient walls is more than a religious experience. It feels like stepping into the opening chapter of a remarkable life.At 15, Rabbi Kook continued his studies in the Panevežys Yeshiva. There, Rabbi Israel Meir Hacohen, known as the Chafetz Chaim, gathered a select group of exceptionally gifted students who were priests and assigned them to immerse themselves in Seder Kodashim, the Talmudic tractates devoted to the Temple service and sacrificial rites. His vision was that when the Messiah came and the Temple was rebuilt, the Jewish people would already have scholars thoroughly versed in its sacred service. Rabbi Kook was chosen to join this elite circle and devoted himself to mastering the laws governing the priests' service in the Holy Temple.The Chafetz Chaim later arranged his marriage to the daughter of Rabbi Eliyahu David Rabinowitz-Teomim (the Aderet), then the rabbi of Panevežys.ŽeimelisAfter his marriage, Rabbi Kook became rabbi of Žeimelis, a quiet agricultural village in northern Lithuania.The countryside has hardly changed. White stone cottages still line the roads. Orange brick farmhouses stand beside wooden barns. Vast flax fields shimmer beneath enormous skies, interrupted only by rows of trees tracing the edges of streams and small lakes. Now and then, herds of deer emerge from the forest and bound gracefully across the open fields.Most of the town's Jewish residents were farmers. For the first time, the brilliant scholar confronted the practical questions of daily agricultural life: The shemita (sabbatical) year restrictions, milking cows on Shabbat, and the countless legal dilemmas of families whose livelihood depended on the land.These encounters profoundly shaped his halachic thinking. The famous heter mechirah, the temporary sale of agricultural land during the sabbatical year, grew from a deep understanding of hardworking farmers whose faith and survival depended equally on the fields before them. Not from abstract legal theory. For Rabbi Kook, Jewish law was never meant to remain confined within the walls of beit midrash. It had to walk through muddy fields, endure rain and drought, and accompany people where life actually unfolded.His former home no longer survives, but its foundations are marked by white stones at Bauskes Street 7.Across from his home, once stood the synagogue where Rabbi Kook studied the Jerusalem Talmud and wrote the first chapters of the book Itur Sofrim, a place that helped shape his intellectual and spiritual world. When I stood among the remaining stones, I found myself regretting that I had not brought a volume of Igrot HaRe'iyah. There seemed no more fitting place to read his words than the place where many of his earliest ideas first took shape.Rabbi Kook lived seven years in Žeimelis, which also witnessed profound personal sorrow. His first wife died here at a young age. Her gravestone, discovered years ago lying abandoned on the ground, has since been restored. The small Jewish cemetery has become another stop for Jewish travelers.Here he remarried. Here his son, Rabbi Zvi Yehuda Kook, was born, later becoming head of Mercaz HaRav Yeshiva and one of the foremost spiritual leaders of religious Zionism (and my rosh yeshiva).Bauska (Boysk)From rural Žeimelis, Rabbi Kook moved to Bauska in southern Latvia. It was an entirely different world. More than half the city's residents were Jewish, yet not all observed Jewish law. Traditional scholars lived alongside merchants, intellectuals, Zionists, laborers, members of the Bund, and young Jews already drifting away from religious life.Years earlier, Rabbi Kook had often traveled to Bauska to study with Rabbi Mordechai Eliasberg, one of the leading figures of the Hibbat Zion movement and an early founder of the Mizrachi movement.When Rabbi Eliasberg passed away, the young Rabbi Kook delivered the eulogy. His words so deeply impressed the community that they immediately offered him the city's rabbinate.He declined.Only five years later did he finally accept.The Jews of Žeimelis loved him so dearly that they reportedly organized a wagon drivers' strike in an attempt to prevent his departure. Eventually, Bauska sent its own drivers, and the young rabbi began the next chapter of his life.The central square of Bauska still looks remarkably similar to photographs from Rabbi Kook's era. Nearby stands a memorial built on the site of his synagogue. The synagogue itself was torched by the Nazis.Today, at Rigas Street, at the corner of Pasta Street, low stone platforms outline its former walls within iron frames. Abstract sculptures stand at the corners. Where the holy ark once stood rises a striking menorah fashioned from stone and iron. At the location of the bimah rests a black monument, shaped like an open book, engraved with the history of Bauska's vanished Jewish community.Currently, there are no Jews in Bauska, but Jewish public buildings such as the school and the slaughterhouse remain and are worth visiting.It was in Bauska that one of Rabbi Kook's most influential ideas fully matured. Ten years he was living in Bauska. He encountered Jews who no longer observed Shabbat and mitzvot, yet he recognized their idealism, their devotion, and their love for the Jewish people and their ancestral homeland. He refused to define them as enemies. To him, even the secular pioneers draining swamps and cultivating barren land were partners in redemption. Their language differed from his; their purpose did not.Following the First Zionist Congress in Basel in 1897, a rumor spread claiming that the Congress had resolved that “Zionism has nothing to do with religion.” (It was later revealed to be fake news, circulated by those whose position had been rejected in the vote).In response, most rabbinic leaders chose to distance themselves from the Zionist movement. Rabbi Kook, however, challenged this approach and argued that there was a better alternative: a religious Zionism that united Jewish faith with Jewish nationhood rather than separating them. The estrangement of today's haredi (ultra-Orthodox) community from compulsory service in the army has its roots in that historic moment, when many came to feel that Zionism was “not ours.”At the age of 39, Rabbi Kook stood at a crossroads. He had to choose between serving as the spiritual supervisor (mashgiach) at the prestigious Telshe Yeshiva, or becoming the rabbi of Jaffa. He chose to make aliyah to Eretz Israel, and the rest is history.Rabbi Kook's contemporaries recognized his extraordinary stature. When derogatory remarks were spoken against him, the Chafetz Chaim reportedly declared that such words warranted the traditional act of rending one's garments in grief. The Chazon Ish likewise refused to join those who opposed Jerusalem's chief rabbi, saying simply: “Know that he is holy and pure.”Returning with different eyesSomething changes after completing this journey. Returning to Rabbi Kook's writings, one no longer encounters abstract ideas alone, but the landscapes that shaped them. Griva inspired his vision, Žeimelis taught agriculture, and Bauska deepened his understanding of sociology. From these quiet towns, he carried to Jaffa and Jerusalem a spiritual vision that sought to unite heaven and earth.Today, most of the synagogues have disappeared, the rabbis' homes are gone, and the communities that once flourished have faded into history. Yet among the birch forests, quiet rivers, and weathered stones, their spirit still lingers. Following Rabbi Kook's footsteps across Latvia and Lithuania is more than a heritage tour. It is a journey to the birthplace of an idea: that faith and modernity, Torah and daily life, can enrich rather than oppose one another.Perhaps that is Rabbi Kook's greatest legacy. Not only the books he wrote, but the hope he carried. His footsteps remind us that every generation can rediscover its past, draw strength from it, and continue the journey toward a brighter future.The author is the creator of the JewishTraveler blog.

Photograph: Raquel Natalicchio/Houston Chronicle/AP ICE (US Immigration and Customs Enforcement) ICE agent who crashed into man in Texas was targeting suspect who died years ago, family says Federal officer slammed vehicle into a construction worker while pursuing a man who died in similar circumstances Associated Press Sat 17 Oct 2026 15.01 EDT Share Prefer the Guardian on Google A federal officer slammed a vehicle into a Houston construction worker and broke his leg , believing him to be a man who apparently died years ago, the dead man’s family said on Friday, further calling into question the account given by US Immigration and Customs Enforcement (ICE). The worker, 48-year-old Miguel Parra Hernandez of Mexico, remains hospitalized with multiple leg fractures and needs reconstructive ankle surgery, according to FIEL, a Houston-based immigration advocacy group. At a news conference on Friday, the group said the alleged suspect’s family had shared documentation proving his death. After the episode on 10 October, ICE said in a statement that officers had observed a suspect they were targeting, identified as Jose Mendoza-Cervantes, enter a vehicle with Parra Hernandez. But on Friday, Rafael Lemaitre, spokesperson with the Harris county district attorney’s office, told the Associated Press that Mendoza-Cervantes was not in that vehicle. ICE did not respond to requests for comment on Friday. “ICE is lying,” said Cesar Espinosa, FIEL’s executive director. “Either somebody is not telling the truth or all of a sudden these two ICE agents have developed a sixth sense and are able to see dead people.” ICE released a photo of a man it identified as Mendoza-Cervantes. But the man in the photo is actually Jose Hector Jimenez, who died years ago while being pursued by federal immigration authorities as he was trying to re-enter the US, according to FIEL. The man’s daughter provided his death certificate from the Mexican government, which has been turned over to the district attorney, Espinosa told the AP. US Customs and Border Protection (CBP) did not respond to a request for comment. Jimenez’s daughter, Jamie Jimenez, did not respond to requests for comment from the AP. Her husband, Andres Rendon, confirmed to the AP that Jimenez was his wife’s deceased father. Criminal charges against the ICE officer who drove the vehicle are being considered by Harris county district attorney Sean Teare, who has said surveillance footage contradicts ICE’s claim that Parra Hernandez stepped in front of the vehicle. The video shows a black SUV speeding over a median and driving toward a man who is running away. The video does not show the car hitting him – that view is blocked by another vehicle – but it shows the SUV inches from the fleeing man. The video then shows him on the ground. US House member Sylvia Garcia, a Democrat who represents Houston, said that ICE appears to be lying about what happened. “If ICE was pursuing a man who died years ago, it raises serious questions about how these operations are being carried out and whether agents are even verifying who they’re looking for before putting people’s lives at risk,” Garcia said in a statement to the AP. “It’s outrageous – but frankly, not surprising.” ICE has been met with nationwide criticism throughout Donald Trump’s second presidency for its aggressive arrest, detention and deportation tactics. Just in 2026, the second year since Trump returned to the White House, more than 30 people have died during interactions with immigration officials, the Guardian reported in late September. Parra Hernandez’s attorney, Kim Bruno, told reporters that her client was suffering from depression in federal custody, especially after learning that he was not the target of the operation. “This never should have happened in the first place,” Bruno said. Miguel’s brother, Roberto Parra, said the two would work construction all day together and he just wants his brother treated with humanity. He said Parra Hernandez has a family to support, and his only crime was coming to a country out of necessity. FIEL is seeking Parra Hernandez’s release before he is moved from a hospital to a federal detention center. Nidia Delfín, the sister of Luis Enrique Delfín, who was detained in the ICE vehicle that hit Parra Hernandez, called for her brother’s release from federal custody so he could serve as a witness. “He’s still very concerned, still very afraid,” she said. “He’s not the same guy that was out” before Parra Hernandez was struck on 10 October.
